faqs.answer: Yes. The assessment on this website is free, runs in your browser, and shows your preliminary results before you are ever asked for contact details. Requesting a personalised review is always optional.
faqs.question: Is the eligibility check really free?

faqs.answer: No — and be cautious of anyone who does. Admissions are decided by universities, scholarships by regional agencies and universities, and visas by Italian authorities. We help you prepare a strong, correct application; outcomes are never guaranteed.
faqs.question: Can you guarantee my admission or scholarship?

faqs.answer: Many English-taught programmes ask for proof of English around B2 level. Some accept IELTS or TOEFL, and some accept a Medium of Instruction (MOI) letter from your previous institution. Accepted proofs differ by programme — always check the official programme page.
faqs.question: Do I need IELTS to study in Italy?

faqs.answer: Diritto allo Studio Universitario (DSU) scholarships are run by Italy's regions for students enrolled at universities in that region. They are assessed mainly on family income and can include a tuition-fee waiver, a cash grant and services like housing and canteens. Deadlines and income rules are set by each region.
faqs.question: What are DSU regional scholarships?

faqs.answer: As early as you can. Programme application windows, scholarship calls and visa appointments run on separate calendars. Starting 9–12 months ahead leaves time for language tests, document legalisation and scholarship applications.
faqs.question: When should I start for the 2027–28 intake?

faqs.answer: Universitaly (the Italian Ministry's portal for international students) is the official starting point for programme search and pre-enrolment. Visa rules are published by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Embassy of Italy in New Delhi.
faqs.question: Where does official information live?

faqs.answer: Use the cost calculator on this website to build your own estimate. As a rough guide, student living costs often fall around €7,000–€11,000 per year depending on the city and housing, plus tuition, which at public universities is income-based. Treat every figure as an estimate, never a quote.
faqs.question: How much does it cost to study in Italy for a year?

faqs.answer: International students with a valid study residence permit are generally allowed part-time work up to 20 hours per week (with an annual cap). Rules can change — verify the current position on official Italian government sources before relying on work income.
faqs.question: Can I work part-time while studying in Italy?

faqs.answer: Start with your passport, academic transcripts and certificates, CV, statement of purpose, recommendation letters where required, and your language proof. For regional scholarships you will also need family income documents, usually translated and legalised. The document checklist page on this site walks through each item.
faqs.question: Which documents should I prepare first?

faqs.answer: After choosing a programme you complete pre-enrolment on the Universitaly portal, then apply for a study visa at the Italian Embassy or consulate responsible for your area, following their published checklist. N92 Edu-Italia helps you prepare and check the file, but the decision is made by the authorities.
faqs.question: How does the student visa process work?

scholarships.benefits: Can combine a tuition-fee waiver with a cash grant and services such as student housing and canteens. Amounts and combinations vary by region and by the student's income band — no amount is stated here because regions publish their own figures each year.
scholarships.closesNote: Set by each region in its annual call — check the regional agency for your university's region.
documents: Proof of enrolment or pre-enrolment at a university in the region

Identity documents and residence details as the regional call specifies
scholarships.geographicEligibility: Students enrolled at a university in the awarding region (each Italian region runs its own scheme).
scholarships.name: Regional Right-to-Study (DSU) Scholarships
scholarships.opensNote: Calls are usually published in summer before the academic year — verify on the regional agency site.
scholarships.procedure: Apply through the regional agency's online portal for the region where your university is located, within that region's call deadline. Admission to the university and the DSU application are separate procedures.
scholarships.provider: Regional right-to-study agencies (e.g. ER.GO — Emilia-Romagna, DSU Toscana, ESU Padova, LazioDisco)
scholarships.requirements: Awarded mainly on family income (ISEE-equivalent assessment for international students); continued eligibility usually requires earning a minimum number of credits (merit condition in later years). Exact thresholds are set by each region's annual call.
scholarships.studentEligibility: Students enrolled (or enrolling) at an Italian university in the region, including international students, subject to the region's income rules.
